column1: # Every container image this project uses, pinned to a digest.
# # Why a digest and not a tag
# A tag is a name someone else can repoint. `debian:13-slim` is a different
# filesystem this month than last, `rust:1.98-slim-bookworm` gets rebuilt when
# its base gets a security update, and `:nonroot` moves whenever distroless
# does. That is the right behaviour for a tag and the wrong one for us twice
# over:
#   - **Reproducibility.** This project builds the same bytes twice on purpose
#     and checks it (`make check-reproducible`). A build whose compiler arrives
#     by mutable name is a build that reproduces until the day it does not, and
#     the change arrives with nobody's commit attached to it.
#   - **Supply chain.** Pulling by tag means running whatever is behind that
#     name at the moment of the pull. Pulling by digest means running the exact
#     bytes written down here, which someone reviewed, and which cannot be
#     swapped without a diff to this file.
# A digest is not a claim that the image has no vulnerabilities. It is a claim
# that the image is the one we looked at. Moving a pin forward is a deliberate
# act with a date on it, which is what the last column is for.
# # How to move one forward
#   scripts/update-image.sh <nickname>
# It re-resolves the tag, shows what changed, and rewrites the line. Run it when
# a base image has a security update worth taking, not on a schedule: an
# unreviewed pull is what the pin exists to prevent.
# # Columns
#   nickname    what scripts/in-container.sh calls it
#   reference   the human-readable tag the digest was resolved from
#   digest      what actually gets run
#   pinned      the date this digest was resolved and reviewed
#   purpose     why this project needs an image at all
# The tag in the second column is *not* what is pulled. It is kept so that a
# person can see what the pin is a pin *of*, and so that update-image.sh knows
# what to re-resolve.
nickname
rust-build
column5: Compiles the broker for its container. The Rust version matches rust-toolchain.toml, because a container that builds with a different compiler than the repository can fail in a way nothing else reproduces.

column1: broker-run
column5: What the broker actually runs on. A C runtime and nothing else: no shell to get, which is the point for the one process strangers can send packets to.

column1: debian
column5: A machine with real dpkg on it. The .deb is assembled here by hand from ar and tar, and Arch has no dpkg to check that against.

column1: fedora
column5: A machine with rpmbuild on it. The spec has been written since Phase 16 opened and had never been built, for want of this.

column1: debian-old
column5: A machine too old to run this. It is here so that the .deb's glibc floor can be shown to bite: a dependency nothing ever refuses is a dependency that proves nothing, and this one was written as a bare `libc6` until a container installed it on bookworm and watched the engine fail to start.
